query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tailored high-entropy alloy (HEA) that incorporates selected catalytically active transition elements into a refractory, multicomponent matrix will exhibit both higher catalytic activity and improved durability for hydrogen evolution (HER) and hydrogen oxidation (HOR) reactions compared to conventional Pt-based catalysts.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional Pt-based electrocatalysts that offer high initial activity but suffer from degradation and durability challenges under harsh electrochemical conditions.
generation.intervention: Design and synthesize a high-entropy alloy via composition engineering, selecting elements that both tune the d-band electronic properties (to enhance hydrogen binding kinetics) and provide robust structural stability (e.g., a NbMoTaW-based matrix with added catalytically active elements such as Ni, Co, or small amounts of Ru).
generation.conditions: Electrochemical environments typical for HER and HOR, such as in 0.5 M H2SO4 (acidic media), under cyclic voltammetry and prolonged operational cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform nanocrystalline microstructure in a single-phase or stable solid solution structure, achieved through controlled synthesis (e.g., sputtering, annealing), which minimizes phase segregation and corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The complex multicomponent composition creates synergistic effects: the tailored d-band center of the active elements enhances hydrogen adsorption/desorption, while the refractory matrix improves corrosion resistance and mitigates dissolution of active sites, collectively overcoming the activity–durability trade-off seen in conventional Pt-based catalysts.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA catalyst is expected to show lower overpotentials and favorable Tafel slopes for HER and HOR along with greater stability and lower degradation rates during extensive cycling relative to commercial Pt-based systems.
generation.baseline: Commercial Pt or Pt-alloy catalysts tested under similar acidic conditions and cycling regimes.
generation.boundary: The performance benefit is anticipated within moderate temperature and pH ranges typical for fuel cell or electrolyzer applications; extreme conditions or significant deviations in processing may alter the microstructure and catalytic behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal alloy composition (i.e., specific elemental ratios) necessary to simultaneously maximize catalytic activity and durability is not precisely known. Additionally, the interplay between microstructural stability and the electronic properties of the active sites requires further systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed HEA with a controlled composition and prepare thin-film electrodes. Conduct electrochemical testing (cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry) in a 0.5 M H2SO4 solution for HER and HOR. Compare the overpotential, Tafel slope, electrochemical active surface area, and durability after extended cycling (e.g., 10,000 cycles) with those of a standard Pt-based catalyst.
measurements: Stability metrics (change in current density and potential over cycling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA catalyst does not demonstrate significantly lower overpotential, comparable or lower Tafel slopes, and improved durability (less performance degradation) relative to the Pt-based catalyst under identical conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. frame.limitation: Current catalysts, such as conventional Pt-based materials, often balance activity with drawbacks like high cost, susceptibility to poisoning, and limited long‐term durability under operating conditions.

decision.trend: Early work with high-entropy and refractory alloys focused on establishing that a complex, multicomponent solid‐solution design can yield exceptional mechanical properties and resistance to harsh environments (oxidation at high temperature, wear, irradiation, etc.). Over time researchers applied controlled processing (from casting to sputtering/annealing) to achieve tailored microstructures and stable interfaces, which improved durability under aggressive conditions. Although these studies were aimed at structural or high‐temperature performance, the underlying design philosophy – achieving stability through composition complexity and controlled microstructuring – is analogous to the challenges faced by electrocatalysts such as Pt for HER/HOR.
decision.unsolved: While the high‐entropy alloy approach has demonstrated impressive durability and stability in structural and high-temperature contexts, its translation into electrocatalytic applications remains unaddressed. In particular, the challenge is to combine high catalytic activity (which depends on finely tuned electronic properties and active sites) with the enhanced durability seen in these alloy systems under corrosive electrochemical conditions.
decision.lever: Design and screen tailored high-entropy alloy compositions that incorporate catalytically active elements (for example, elements known to modulate d-band structures favorable for HER/HOR) while leveraging the inherent stability of multicomponent alloys
decision.why: Given the trend that complex alloy compositions can create synergistic effects that improve material stability in harsh environments, the next logical step is to apply a composition‐engineering strategy. By carefully selecting and balancing elements to both activate hydrogen reactions and resist dissolution/poisoning, researchers can potentially achieve a catalyst that overcomes the activity–durability trade-off seen in conventional Pt-based systems.
